learningJourney.title: Delta-of-Delta timestamps & Gorilla XOR float compression

explanation.foundation: Think of **Delta-of-Delta timestamps & Gorilla XOR float compression** as the intuition layer for Time-Series Databases: Establishes the core invariant and production trade-off behind delta-of-delta timestamps & gorilla xor float compression.
explanation.core: Because scrape intervals are regular (e.g., every 10s), second-order timestamp deltas are near zero—compressing 64-bit timestamps to ~1–2 bits each.
explanation.deepDive: Under heavy load or partial failure, delta-of-delta timestamps & gorilla xor float compression becomes a critical lever for predictable latency and correctness. Learn how time-series engines achieve 10x+ compression and millions of writes/sec using time-partitioned chunks, Gorilla/Delta encoding, and downsampling.

learningJourney.markdownContent:
```python
# Delta-of-delta timestamp encoding concept (Python)
def delta_of_delta(timestamps: list[int]) -> list[int]:
    deltas = [timestamps[i] - timestamps[i - 1] for i in range(1, len(timestamps))]
    return [deltas[0]] + [deltas[i] - deltas[i - 1] for i in range(1, len(deltas))]
# Regular 10s scrapes [1000, 1010, 1020, 1030] -> dod: [10, 0, 0]!
```

decisionFramework.problem: How to implement Time-Series Databases without hitting unbounded tail latency, state divergence, or operational fragility.
decisionFramework.naiveSolution: Use a single unpartitioned path with unbounded retries and synchronous global coordination.
decisionFramework.whyItFails: Global coordination serializes throughput under load, while unbounded retries amplify transient stalls into full outages.
decisionFramework.alternatives: Compare synchronous strict-consistency paths against bounded asynchronous replication, local caching, or partitioned ownership.
decisionFramework.decision: When concurrent writes contend on shared state, time-series workloads are append-mostly, immutable, and queried over recent time windows—allowing specialized columnar compression and retention drops.
decisionFramework.tradeOffs: Gains predictable p99 latency and fault isolation in exchange for explicit bounding, observability, and slightly higher implementation complexity.

options.label: Increase retry counts and remove client timeouts so every request eventually succeeds.
options.explanation: Unbounded retries multiply load on an already struggling dependency and exhaust worker pools.

options.label: Enforce strict latency budgets, bounded jittered retries, and graceful fallback or load shedding.
options.explanation: Bounding retries and isolating slow paths preserves healthy capacity and keeps tail latency predictable.

tabbedExplorer.name: Cardinality Bomb
tabbedExplorer.title: Inverted Index Memory Exhaustion
tabbedExplorer.desc: Putting unbounded IDs (`user_id`, `request_id`, `trace_id`) into indexed tags creates millions of unique series, blowing up RAM.
tabbedExplorer.rule: Keep indexed tags low-cardinality (<100K active series/shard); put high-cardinality IDs in logs/traces or unindexed fields.

tabbedExplorer.name: Downsampling
tabbedExplorer.title: Raw Short-TTL + Aggregated Rollups
tabbedExplorer.desc: Keep 10s raw samples for 7 days, 5m rollups for 90 days, and 1h rollups for 2+ years.
tabbedExplorer.rule: Store pre-aggregated `sum` + `count` (or histograms/DDSketch) rather than averaging pre-computed averages or percentiles.

qaDetails.summary: Why can you never average p99 latencies across servers or time buckets?
qaDetails.body: Percentiles are non-additive. Store mergeable histograms (HDRHistogram / DDSketch / Prometheus native histograms) so p99 can be accurately aggregated across shards and windows.

qaDetails.summary: How do TSDBs handle out-of-order / late-arriving IoT samples?
qaDetails.body: Modern TSDBs buffer recent out-of-order samples in a mutable head/WAL window and merge them during chunk compaction, rejecting samples older than a bounded grace window.

learningJourney.whyThisMatters: Establishes the core invariant and production trade-off behind late-arriving samples & averaging percentiles.

knowledgeCheck.question: Why does adding `user_id` as an indexed tag in Prometheus or InfluxDB often crash the TSDB?

options.text: A. Integers cannot be compressed by Gorilla
options.feedback: Tags are metadata labels, not the metric value itself.

options.text: B. Cardinality explosion: every unique tag combination creates a new time series in the RAM inverted index
options.feedback: Correct! Millions of unique user_ids create millions of active series, exhausting index memory and causing OOM.

options.text: C. Disks cannot store more than 100 tables
options.feedback: Series are stored in chunk files and inverted indexes, not separate SQL tables.

tipsAndTricks: Never put unbounded IDs (user_id, request_id, URL path with IDs) in indexed TSDB tags.
Store mergeable histograms (or sum + count) instead of pre-computed p99s or averages so rollups remain mathematically valid.
Use time-based chunk partitioning so retention cleanup is an instant file drop rather than expensive row-by-row DELETEs.
finalSummaryEyebrow: The idea to keep with you
finalSummaryTitle: Bound tag cardinality, partition by time chunks, and downsample older metrics automatically.
